This vignette maps out the complete pipeline for calibrating self-reported anthropometric survey data (such as height and weight from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey) using continuous, measured reference distributions from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). 

By evaluating continuous age as a flexible natural spline instead of using arbitrary age brackets, the functions borrow statistical strength across the distribution spectrum to smooth out digit preference heaping and reconstruct truncated upper tails.

## 1. Setting Up the Target and Reference Data

In a standard analysis workflow, you will read in your raw data frames directly from AHRQ and CDC repositories. For this guide, we generate a synthetic framework to mirror common survey artifacts:

```r
library(mepsCalibrate)
library(mgcv)

set.seed(101)
n_records <- 1500

# Synthetic NHANES Reference (Measured, Un-truncated)
nhanes_df <- data.frame(
  age   = runif(n_records, 18, 85),
  sex   = sample(c("M", "F"), n_records, replace = TRUE),
  race  = sample(c("White", "Black", "Hispanic"), n_records, replace = TRUE),
  weight_measured = 130 + rnorm(n_records, 30, 15)
)

# Synthetic MEPS Target (Self-reported, Rounded, Top-Coded at 250 lbs)
meps_df <- data.frame(
  age   = runif(n_records, 18, 85),
  sex   = sample(c("M", "F"), n_records, replace = TRUE),
  race  = sample(c("White", "Black", "Hispanic"), n_records, replace = TRUE)
)
true_weights <- 125 + rnorm(n_records, 28, 15)
meps_df$weight_reported <- round(true_weights / 5) * 5 # Digit heaping
meps_df$weight_reported[meps_df$weight_reported >= 250] <- 250 # Truncation Wall
meps_df$mortality <- rbinom(n_records, 1, 0.05) # Target outcome
```

## 2. Running the Stratified Calibration Pipeline

The `meps_calibrate_pipeline` function automates the demographic partitioning. It splits the tables by your specified `strata_vars`, extracts smooth continuous quantile grids using natural age splines on the anchor dataset, and maps the target data directly into continuous U(0,1) copula space.

```r
meps_df$calibrated_weight_p <- meps_calibrate_pipeline(
  meps_data      = meps_df,
  nhanes_data    = nhanes_df,
  reported_var   = "weight_reported",
  measured_var   = "weight_measured",
  truncation_val = 250,
  strata_vars    = c("sex", "race"),
  df             = 3
)
```

## 3. Modeling the Overall Height-by-Weight Landscape

Because the resulting vector is transformed into a continuous uniform coordinate system free of reporting heaps or truncation cliffs, you can plug it straight into localized spline engines. Decomposing the space into main effects and pure interactions (`ti`) allows you to isolate departures from the homogeneity assumption without your curves chasing behavioral noise:

```r
# Fit a piecewise exponential survival structure or a flexible GAM
height_weight_gam <- gam(
  mortality ~ s(age) + ti(calibrated_weight_p, k = 6),
  family = binomial(),
  data = meps_df,
  method = "REML"
)

summary(height_weight_gam)
```
